## Operations are element-wise

```python
x = np.arange(5)   # [0 1 2 3 4]

x ** 2             # [0 1 4 9 16]
x + 10             # [10 11 12 13 14]
np.sqrt(x)         # no loop

t * t              # element-wise
t @ t.T            # matrix product
```

::: notes
Every arithmetic operator and every `np.` maths function applies to each element: this
is vectorization, and it is the whole style of numpy, pandas and torch. If you write a
`for` loop over the elements of an array, there is almost always a one-liner instead.
Careful with `*`: on arrays it multiplies element by element. The matrix product is `@`.
Compare with lists: `[1, 2] * 2` is `[1, 2, 1, 2]`, and `[1, 2] + [3]` concatenates.
Same symbol, different type, different meaning.
:::

## Functions

![](img/function_anatomy.png)

::: notes
`def` creates a function; calling it runs the body with the arguments bound to the
parameters, and `return` hands a value back to the caller.
Insist on the difference between printing and returning: `print` shows a value to a human
and gives nothing back, `return` produces a value the rest of the program can use. A
function that prints its result cannot be reused.
Default arguments (`skip_none=True`) give an option without forcing every caller to think
about it. Keyword arguments at the call site (`mean(values, skip_none=False)`) are worth
the extra characters: in six months, that line still says what it does.
Scope in one sentence: names created inside the function disappear when it returns.
:::

## Two names, one list

![](img/aliasing.png)

::: notes
Back to the first picture: `b = a` sticks a second label on the same list. It does not
copy. Appending through `b` is visible through `a`, because there is only one list.
This matters as soon as they pass a list to a function, or take a "copy" of a table to
clean it. `.copy()` (or `list(a)`, or `a[:]`) makes an independent list.
Strings, numbers and tuples are immutable, so sharing them is harmless: nothing can
change them in place. The trap only exists for mutable values: lists, dicts, sets.
:::

## Accumulating a result

```python
total = 0
for hr in heart_rates:
    total = total + hr

mean = total / len(heart_rates)
```

::: notes
The accumulator pattern: a variable created *before* the loop, updated *inside* it, used
*after* it. Sum, count, maximum, a list being built: they are all this shape.
Create it before the loop, or the name does not exist yet; `total = 0` for a sum,
`best = values[0]` for a maximum (not 0, which breaks on negative values).
They will do this by hand in the notebook, then meet `sum`, `max` and `np.mean`, which do
the same thing faster and with less room for error. Writing it once by hand is what makes
the shortcut readable afterwards.
:::
083b5ea78092.fr:
## Accumuler un résultat

```python
total = 0
for hr in heart_rates:
    total = total + hr

mean = total / len(heart_rates)
```

::: notes
Le modèle d'accumulateur : une variable créée *avant* la boucle, mise à jour *à l'intérieur* de celle-ci, utilisée
*après* ça. Somme, décompte, maximum, une liste en construction : ils ont tous cette forme.
Créez-le avant la boucle, sinon le nom n'existe pas encore ; `total = 0` pour une somme,
`best = values[0]` pour un maximum (et non 0, qui casse sur des valeurs négatives).
Ils le feront à la main dans le cahier, puis rencontreront `sum`, `max` et `np.mean`, qui font
la même chose plus rapidement et avec moins de marge d’erreur. L'écrire une fois à la main est ce qui fait
le raccourci lisible par la suite.

08f83edf1f84.en:
## Dictionaries: `dict`

![](img/dict_record.png)

::: notes
A dict maps keys to values: a record where each field has a name. `patient["age"]` is
clearer than `patient[1]`, and stays correct when a field is added.
Missing keys raise a `KeyError`. Two ways to cope: test first with `in`, or use `.get` with
a default. Prefer `.get` when a missing field is normal (smoking status often is).
Lookup by key is instantaneous whatever the size of the dict; that is why dicts are
also used to count things: `counts[d] = counts.get(d, 0) + 1`.
Loop with `for key, value in patient.items():`.
:::
08f83edf1f84.fr:
## Dictionnaires : `dict`

![](img/dict_record.png)

::: notes
Un dict mappe les clés aux valeurs : un enregistrement où chaque champ a un nom. `patient["age"]` est
plus clair que `patient[1]` et reste correct lorsqu'un champ est ajouté.
Les clés manquantes génèrent un `KeyError`. Deux façons de gérer : testez d'abord avec `in`, ou utilisez `.get` avec

0aa414085b37.en:
## The methods Python calls for you

| Method | Called by | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `__init__(self, ...)` | `Patient("P001", 54)` | store the attributes |
| `__repr__(self)` | the object displayed, `print` | a readable `Patient('P001', 54 y)` |
| `__len__(self)` | `len(ward)` | how many patients |
| `__eq__(self, other)` | `a == b` | same patient id |
| `__getitem__(self, k)` | `ward[0]` | make it indexable |

::: notes
The double-underscore names ("dunder") are not magic syntax: they are ordinary methods
that Python calls on your behalf when an operator or a built-in is used. Defining them is
how your class behaves like a built-in type.
`__repr__` is the one to write every time, on day one. Without it the notebook shows
`<__main__.Patient object at 0x7f3c...>`, which tells them nothing; with it, debugging a
list of objects becomes readable. Put the identifying fields in it, not everything.
`__len__` must return an integer, and it also decides truthiness: with `__len__` defined,
an empty ward is falsy, so `if ward:` works (Session 1 again).
`__eq__` is worth a word of caution in health data: two measurements of the same patient
are not the same object, and equality on floats is still a bad idea. Compare ids.
They are not asked to memorise the list, only to recognise the pattern: if a built-in
should work on their object, there is a dunder for it.
::: -->

## Missing values and types

```python
df.isna().sum()                  # how many NaN per column

clean = df.dropna()              # keep only the complete rows
len(df), len(clean)              # 240, 232

clean["age"] = clean["age"].astype("int64")
clean["ward"] = clean["ward"].astype("category")
clean["admission"] = pd.to_datetime(clean["admission"])
```

::: notes
`isna()` gives a table of True/False, and `.sum()` counts the True per column: the missing
value report of the export, in one line.
`dropna()` removes every row with at least one missing value. It is the simplest choice,
not always the right one: here it costs 8 patients out of 240. `dropna(subset=["age"])`
drops only on the column that matters, and `fillna(value)` replaces instead of dropping.
Whatever you choose, say it in the methods section.
Once the NaN are gone, `astype("int64")` gives back a real integer age. `"category"` is for
a column with few distinct values (the ward, the outcome): less memory, and it says that
these are groups. `pd.to_datetime` turns the admission text into real dates, which can be
subtracted and sorted.
:::

## Lists: `list`

```python
heart_rates = [72, 85, 64, 90, 78]
heart_rates[0]       # 72
heart_rates[1:4]     # [85, 64, 90]

heart_rates.append(101)   # at the end
heart_rates[1] = 80       # by position
heart_rates.remove(64)    # by value

sum(heart_rates) / len(heart_rates)
[hr for hr in heart_rates if hr > 80]
```

::: notes
Same indexing and slicing as strings: they already know it. The difference is that a list
can change in place.
`min`, `max`, `sum` and `len` work on any list of numbers.
The last line is a list comprehension: "the hr, for each hr in heart_rates, if hr > 80".
Read it in that order. It is the Python way to filter and transform, and it is the shape
of what pandas will do on a whole column.
`sorted(x)` returns a new sorted list; `x.sort()` sorts in place and returns `None`.
Assigning the result of `.sort()` is a classic bug.
:::

## Booleans and comparisons

```python
temp = 38.4

36.5 <= temp <= 37.5   # False
fever = temp >= 38     # True
fever and not False    # True

type(fever)            # bool
True + True            # 2
```

::: notes
Comparisons produce booleans, and booleans are what `if` and filters consume.
The chained comparison is a Python nicety that reads like maths; most languages need
`temp >= 36.5 and temp <= 37.5`.
`True + True == 2` is a curiosity now, but it is useful later: `sum(fevers)` counts the
patients with a fever, and `mean` of a boolean column is a proportion.
Note `=` (assign) versus `==` (compare): the most common typo of the week.
:::
1267fb2701d9.fr:
## Booléens et comparaisons

```python

36.5 <= temp <= 37.5   # False
fever = temp >= 38     # True
fever and not False    # True

type(fever)            # bool
True + True            # 2
```

::: notes
Les comparaisons produisent des booléens, et les booléens sont ce que `if` et les filtres consomment.
La comparaison chaînée est une subtilité Python qui se lit comme des mathématiques ; la plupart des langues ont besoin
`temp >= 36.5 and temp <= 37.5`.
`True + True == 2` est une curiosité maintenant, mais il sera utile plus tard : `sum(fevers)` compte le
les patients ayant de la fièvre, et `mean` d'une colonne booléenne est une proportion.

23838d77ca27.en:
## Numbers: `int` and `float`

![](img/numbers.png)

::: notes
`int` is exact and has no maximum: `2 ** 100` just works, Python grows the integer as
needed. `float` is a 64 bit approximation: about 16 significant digits, and a maximum
near 1.8e308 (`2.0 ** 1024` overflows).
`0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3` surprises everyone once. It is not a Python bug: 0.1 has no exact
binary form, exactly as 1/3 has no exact decimal form. Every language does this.
The rule to take away: compare floats with `math.isclose`, never with `==`. A lab value
filter written with `==` on floats will silently drop rows.
:::

3182b2a35f78.en:
## Order of tests

![](img/branching.png)

::: notes
With `elif`, Python tests from top to bottom and stops at the first true test: the rest
is never evaluated. So each `elif` silently means "and none of the tests above matched",
which is exactly why `sbp < 120` does not need to repeat `and sbp >= 90`.
The classic bug is on the right: a wider test placed first swallows the narrower ones,
and every patient below 130 comes out "elevated". Nothing crashes, the numbers are just
wrong, which is the dangerous kind of bug.
The rule: for thresholds, go from the narrowest to the widest, and let `else` catch what
is left.
:::

3182b2a35f78.fr:
## Ordre des tests

![](img/branching.png)

::: notes
Avec `elif`, Python teste de haut en bas et s'arrête au premier vrai test : le reste
n’est jamais évalué. Ainsi, chaque `elif` signifie silencieusement "et aucun des tests ci-dessus ne correspond",
c'est exactement pourquoi `sbp < 120` n'a pas besoin de répéter `and sbp >= 90`.
Le bug classique est à droite : un test plus large placé en premier avale les plus étroits,
et chaque patient en dessous de 130 en sort « élevé ». Rien ne plante, les chiffres sont juste
faux, ce qui est un type de bug dangereux.
La règle : pour les seuils, allez du plus étroit au plus large, et laissez `else` attraper quoi
est laissé.
:::

## A class is a blueprint

![](img/class_anatomy.png)

::: notes
They have been using objects since Session 1 without the word: a `str` has `.upper()`, a
list has `.append()`. A class is how you define your own type, for data that travels
together.
`__init__` runs at creation and stores the attributes on `self`; `self` is simply the
object the method was called on, and it is the first parameter of every method. `p.bmi()`
is just `Patient.bmi(p)`.
The names with double underscores are hooks Python calls for you: `__init__` at creation,
`__repr__` when the object is displayed, `__len__` for `len(obj)`. Define `__repr__`
early, it turns an unreadable `<object at 0x7f...>` into something they can debug with.
Two objects of the same class are independent: changing `q.weight` leaves `p` untouched.
:::

## Every value is true or false

![](img/truthy.png)

::: notes
Any value can stand in an `if`. Zero and empty are false, everything else is true.
This gives short, idiomatic code (`if heart_rates:` instead of `if len(heart_rates) > 0:`),
and one classic trap: the string `"0"` read from a CSV is truthy, because it is a
non-empty string. Convert before you test.
:::

![](img/truthy.png)

## Saving

```python
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("fig1.png", dpi=300)
fig.savefig("fig1.pdf")
fig.savefig("fig1.svg")

plt.close(fig)    # in loops
```

::: notes
The format is chosen by the extension. PNG is an image: choose a `dpi` high enough for the
final size (300 for print). PDF and SVG are vector formats: lines and text stay sharp at
any zoom, and journals ask for them.
Save from code, never with a screenshot: the figure is then reproducible, and regenerating
it after a data correction is one command.
In a loop that makes a figure per patient, `plt.close(fig)` frees the memory; otherwise
matplotlib keeps them all and warns after 20.

## Selecting

```python
clean["age"]                     # one column, a Series
clean["age"].mean()              # 50.9
clean["ward"].value_counts()     # how many patients per ward

summary = clean[["patient_id", "age"]]  # a smaller DataFrame
```

::: notes
One name in the brackets gives a Series, which carries the usual statistics as methods:
`mean`, `median`, `std`, `min`, `max`, `describe`.

of patients per ward, per outcome, per sex, sorted, in one call.

the double brackets: the outer ones are the selection, the inner ones are the list.
Selecting rows instead of columns is a condition: `clean[clean["ward"] == "ICU"]`, exactly
the boolean masks of Session 3, applied to a table.
:::

4391d9ca0e43.en:
## Arithmetic operators

| Expression | Result | Type |
|---|---|---|
| `7 + 2`, `7 - 2`, `7 * 2` | `9`, `5`, `14` | `int` |
| `7 / 2` | `3.5` | `float`, always |
| `7 // 2` | `3` | `int` (floor division) |
| `7 % 2` | `1` | `int` (remainder) |
| `7 ** 2` | `49` | `int` (power) |
| `round(3.14159, 2)` | `3.14` | `float` |

::: notes
The one to underline: `/` always returns a float, even for `6 / 2` (gives `3.0`).
`//` and `%` go together: "how many full groups, and what is left over". Example:
`minutes // 60` and `minutes % 60` turn a stay duration into hours and minutes.
`int(3.9)` is 3: `int` truncates, it does not round. Use `round` when you mean round.
:::

## Four containers

![](img/containers.png)

::: notes
Three questions decide which container to use.
(1) Do I find items by position, or by name? Position: list or tuple. Name: dict.
(2) Will it change? A list grows as measurements arrive; a tuple is a fixed record,
  like (systolic, diastolic).
(3) Do duplicates matter? A set keeps each value once, which is exactly "the distinct
  medications".
Literal syntax: square brackets for lists, parentheses for tuples, braces for dicts and
sets (braces with `key: value` pairs make a dict). Careful: `{}` is an empty dict; an
empty set is `set()`.
:::

## `range` and `enumerate`

![](img/loop_helpers_a.png)

::: notes
`range(stop)`, `range(start, stop)`, `range(start, stop, step)`: the counted loop, used
when the number of turns is the point and the items are not. Note `range(5)` stops at 4,
like a slice, and that `range` builds nothing: it hands out the numbers one at a time,
which is why `range(10_000_000)` is instant and costs no memory.
`enumerate` when you need the position as well as the value: it gives a pair each turn,
unpacked into two names exactly like `a, b = 1, 2` in Session 1. Start elsewhere with
`enumerate(hrs, start=1)` when you want to count from 1 for a human reader.
If they find themselves writing `for i in range(len(hrs))` and then `hrs[i]`, `enumerate`
is what they wanted.
:::
4f4d1b888dbe.fr:
## `range` et `enumerate`

![](img/loop_helpers_a.png)

::: notes
`range(stop)`, `range(start, stop)`, `range(start, stop, step)` : la boucle comptée, utilisée
lorsque le nombre de tours est important et que les objets ne le sont pas. Notez que `range(5)` s'arrête à 4,
comme une tranche, et ce `range` ne construit rien : il distribue les nombres un à un,

`enumerate` quand on a besoin de la position ainsi que de la valeur : ça donne une paire à chaque tour,
décomposé en deux noms exactement comme `a, b = 1, 2` dans la session 1. Commencez ailleurs avec
`enumerate(hrs, start=1)` quand on veut compter à partir de 1 pour un lecteur humain.
S'ils se retrouvent à écrire `for i in range(len(hrs))` puis `hrs[i]`, `enumerate`
c'est ce qu'ils voulaient.

556bf0f53d57.en:
## Dictionary or class?

```python
# dict: data only
p = {"id": "P001", "age": 54}
p["age"]


# class: data + behaviour
class Patient:
    def bmi(self): ...
p.bmi()
```

::: notes
Honest answer: for a handful of fields read once from a CSV, a dict is fine, and that is
what pandas will give them anyway.
A class earns its place when behaviour belongs with the data (a BMI computed from the
patient's own fields), when the same shape is created many times, or when you want a
guarantee that every object has the same attributes, which a dict never gives you: a
typo in a key creates a new key instead of an error.
:::
556bf0f53d57.fr:
## Dictionnaire ou classe ?

```python
# dict: data only
p = {"id": "P001", "age": 54}
p["age"]


# class: data + behaviour
class Patient:
    def bmi(self): ...
p.bmi()
```

::: notes
Réponse honnête : pour une poignée de champs lus une fois à partir d'un CSV, un dict suffit, et c'est
ce que les pandas leur donneront de toute façon.
Une classe gagne sa place lorsque le comportement appartient aux données (un IMC calculé à partir de la

## `zip` and `.items()`

![](img/loop_helpers_b.png)

::: notes
`zip` walks two (or more) sequences in step: ids and temperatures, heights and weights,
measured and predicted. Again a pair per turn, unpacked into two names.
One trap worth saying out loud: `zip` stops at the shortest sequence, silently. If the ids
and the temperatures do not have the same length, the extra ones are dropped without a
word, so check `len` first when the two come from different files.
`.items()` does the same for a dictionary, giving the key and the value; `.keys()` and
`.values()` exist when only one of them is needed. Iterating a dict directly gives the
keys alone, which is a common surprise.
These four helpers cover almost every loop they will write this year.
:::
5be529f3cbb1.fr:
## `zip` et `.items()`

![](img/loop_helpers_b.png)

::: notes
`zip` parcourt deux (ou plus) séquences pas à pas : identifiants et températures, tailles et poids,
mesuré et prédit. Encore une paire par tour, décomposée en deux noms.
Un piège qui mérite d'être dit à voix haute : `zip` s'arrête à la séquence la plus courte, en silence. Si les identifiants
et les températures n'ont pas la même longueur, les températures supplémentaires tombent sans
mot, alors vérifiez d'abord `len` lorsque les deux proviennent de fichiers différents.
`.items()` fait la même chose pour un dictionnaire, en donnant la clé et la valeur ; `.keys()` et
`.values()` existent lorsqu'un seul d'entre eux est nécessaire. Itérer un dict donne directement le
clés seules, ce qui est une surprise courante.
Ces quatre assistants couvrent presque toutes les boucles qu’ils écriront cette année.
:::

5d51e41bdb67.en:
## Lists are slow for numbers

![](img/list_vs_array.png)

::: notes
A list of a million heart rates is a million separate Python objects, each with its own
type, scattered in memory; the list only holds arrows to them. Every `+` in a loop asks
Python "what type is this?" again.
A NumPy array is one contiguous block of numbers, all of the same type (the dtype). The
loop is then run by compiled C code, which never asks: that is the "Fast" panel of
Session 0, made concrete.
The price: an array holds one type only, and has a fixed size. For numbers, that is the
price you always want to pay. Measure it yourself in the notebook with `%timeit`.
:::
5d51e41bdb67.fr:
## Les listes sont lentes pour les chiffres

![](img/list_vs_array.png)

::: notes

tapez, dispersés dans la mémoire; la liste ne contient que des flèches. Chaque `+` dans une boucle demande
Python "de quel type s'agit-il ?" encore.
Un tableau NumPy est un bloc contigu de nombres, tous du même type (le dtype). Le
la boucle est ensuite exécutée par du code C compilé, qui ne demande jamais : c'est le panneau "Rapide" de
Séance 0, rendue concrète.
Le prix : un tableau ne contient qu’un seul type et a une taille fixe. Pour les chiffres, c'est le
prix que vous voulez toujours payer. Mesurez-le vous-même dans le cahier avec `%timeit`.

5fd77853ecf3.en:
## Colour maps

![](img/colormap_choice.png)

::: notes
One smooth field (think a perfusion map, mL/100 g/min), one window
(`vmin=0, vmax=80`): everything that changes between these eight panels is the colour
map, and so is everything the reader sees. The data has no edge anywhere; every ring and
every band below was added by the colour map.
gray is the convention for CT, MRI and X-ray: radiologists read grey levels, and a
colourful slice looks wrong to them. bone is the same idea with a cold tint.
viridis and magma are the default choices for a measured quantity (perfusion, dose,
activation, a correlation matrix): brightness increases with the value, so they survive
printing in black and white and colour blindness.
RdBu_r and coolwarm are for a difference: post minus pre, patient minus atlas, a
correlation. They need `vmin=-v, vmax=v` so the white is exactly 0. On raw data, where
no value is special, they invent a centre that does not exist, which is what you see here.
jet and nipy_spectral put bands and bright spots where the data is smooth. They are still
the default in a lot of medical software; change them.
Rule of thumb: one quantity going up, sequential (gray, viridis); a signed difference,
diverging centred on 0; categories (segmentation labels), a qualitative map such as
tab10 with `imshow` and no colorbar.
:::
5fd77853ecf3.fr:
## Cartes de couleurs

![](img/colormap_choice.png)

::: notes
Un champ lisse (pensez à une carte de perfusion, mL/100 g/min), une fenêtre
(`vmin=0, vmax=80`) : tout ce qui change entre ces huit panneaux c'est la couleur
carte, tout comme tout ce que le lecteur voit. Les données n’ont aucun avantage nulle part ; chaque sonnerie et
chaque bande ci-dessous a été ajoutée par la carte des couleurs.
le gris est la convention pour la tomodensitométrie, l'IRM et les rayons X : les radiologues lisent les niveaux de gris et un
la tranche colorée ne leur semble pas bonne. l'os est la même idée avec une teinte froide.
viridis et magma sont les choix par défaut pour une quantité mesurée (perfusion, dose,
activation, une matrice de corrélation) : la luminosité augmente avec la valeur, donc ils survivent
impression en noir et blanc et daltonisme.
RdBu_r et coolwarm font la différence : post moins pré, patient moins atlas, a
corrélation. Ils ont besoin de `vmin=-v, vmax=v` pour que le blanc soit exactement 0. Sur les données brutes, où
aucune valeur n'est spéciale, ils inventent un centre qui n'existe pas, c'est ce que vous voyez ici.
jet et nipy_spectral placent des bandes et des points lumineux là où les données sont fluides. Ils sont encore
la valeur par défaut dans de nombreux logiciels médicaux ; changez-les.
Règle générale : une quantité croissante, séquentielle (gris, viridis) ; une différence signée,
divergent centré sur 0 ; catégories (étiquettes de segmentation), une carte qualitative telle que
tab10 avec `imshow` et pas de barre de couleurs.
:::

60235190068b.en:
## Broadcasting

![](img/broadcasting.png)

::: notes
When the shapes differ, numpy stretches the smaller array along the missing axis, as if
it were repeated (it is not actually copied). `x + 10` was already broadcasting: a scalar
stretched to every cell.
The rule: compare shapes from the right; each pair of sizes must be equal, or one of them
must be 1. `(3, 4)` and `(4,)` match. `(3, 4)` and `(3,)` do not: to add one value per
row, make it a column, shape `(3, 1)`, with `.reshape(3, 1)` or `v[:, None]`.
Typical use: subtracting the mean of each column from a table, in one line.
:::
60235190068b.fr:
## Diffusion

![](img/broadcasting.png)

::: notes
Lorsque les formes diffèrent, numpy étend le plus petit tableau le long de l'axe manquant, comme si
il a été répété (il n’est pas réellement copié). `x + 10` diffusait déjà : un scalaire
étendu à chaque cellule.
La règle : comparer les formes en partant de la droite ; chaque paire de tailles doit être égale, ou l'une d'elles
doit être 1. `(3, 4)` et `(4,)` correspondent. `(3, 4)` et `(3,)` ne le font pas : pour ajouter une valeur par
ligne, faites-en une colonne, formez `(3, 1)`, avec `.reshape(3, 1)` ou `v[:, None]`.
Utilisation typique : soustraire la moyenne de chaque colonne d'un tableau, sur une seule ligne.
:::

627b6422b422.en:
## Low level, high level

![](img/levels.png)

::: notes
A language is a level of description. Machine code is what the processor runs: numbers.
Assembly is the same thing with names, one instruction per line. C, C++ and Rust let you
write expressions, but you still decide where every byte lives. Python lets you write the
thing you meant, and decides the rest for you.
Low level buys control and speed, and costs lines of code and bugs (every buffer and every
pointer is yours to get right). High level buys time, and costs some control.
Nothing here is "better": they sit at different points of the same trade.
:::
627b6422b422.fr:
## Niveau bas, niveau haut

![](img/levels.png)

::: notes
Une langue est un niveau de description. Le code machine est ce que le processeur exécute : des nombres.
L'assemblage est la même chose avec les noms, une instruction par ligne. C, C++ et Rust vous permettent
écrivez des expressions, mais vous décidez toujours où se trouve chaque octet. Python vous permet d'écrire le
ce que vous vouliez dire, et décide du reste pour vous.
Un niveau bas achète du contrôle et de la vitesse, et coûte des lignes de code et des bugs (chaque tampon et chaque
le pointeur est à vous pour bien faire). Un niveau élevé fait gagner du temps et coûte un certain contrôle.
Rien ici n'est « meilleur » : ils siègent à différents points d'un même métier.
:::

## Comprehensions

![](img/comprehension.png)

::: notes
A comprehension is the same loop written as one expression: what to keep, where it comes
from, and optionally which ones. Python reads it in that order, and so should they.
It is the idiomatic way to transform a list into another list, and it shows up constantly
in real code, so they must be able to read one even if they prefer writing loops.
The limit: a comprehension builds a collection. A loop that prints, writes a file or
calls a service stays a loop. And a comprehension with two `for` and three `if` should go
back to being a loop.
:::
65899df07dc6.fr:
## Compréhensions

![](img/comprehension.png)

::: notes
Une compréhension est la même boucle écrite comme une seule expression : quoi garder, d'où cela vient
de, et éventuellement lesquels. Python le lit dans cet ordre, et il devrait en être de même.
C'est la manière idiomatique de transformer une liste en une autre liste, et elle apparaît constamment
en code réel, ils doivent donc être capables d'en lire un même s'ils préfèrent écrire des boucles.
La limite : une compréhension construit une collection. Une boucle qui imprime, écrit un fichier ou
les appels à un service restent une boucle. Et une compréhension avec deux `for` et trois `if` devrait aller
redevenu une boucle.
:::

## History and branches

![](img/git_history.png)

::: notes
Each commit has an identifier (a hash, shortened to 7 characters) and points to the
commit before it: the history is a chain.
A branch is just a name on a commit, moving forward as you commit. `git switch -c new-plot`
starts one: try an idea without touching `main`. If it works, `git merge new-plot` brings
it back; if not, delete the branch and `main` never knew.

match that snapshot. Nothing is lost: every commit is still there.

## One style, decided by a tool

```bash
$ uv venv
# create .venv
$ source .venv/bin/activate # unix
> .venv\Scripts\activate # windows

$ uv pip install ruff
# or: uv add --dev ruff

$ ruff --version
```

::: notes
`ruff` is a formatter *and* a linter for Python, from the same people as `uv`, so it
installs the same way and runs just as fast (a whole project in well under a second).
Two jobs, worth separating in their heads:
(1) the formatter rewrites the layout of your code: indentation, quotes, line breaks,
  spaces around operators. It never changes what the code does.
(2) the linter reads the code and reports mistakes: an unused import, a variable
  assigned and never read, a name that does not exist.
Why bother in a health-data project? Because a diff should show what you changed, not
who reformatted it. With a formatter, `git diff` contains only real changes, and code
review stops being an argument about spaces.
Note `uv add --dev ruff`: it is a development tool, not a dependency of the analysis, so
it belongs in the dev group of `pyproject.toml`.
If `ruff` is not on the path, run it through uv: `uv run ruff --version`.
:::

78f126b2b7a2.en:
## Colour maps

![](img/colormaps.png)

::: notes
A colour map encodes a number; the eye must read it as a number.
Sequential maps (viridis, the default, or gray) go from dark to light: brightness increases
with the value, even printed in black and white, and for colour-blind readers (about 1 man
in 12).
Diverging maps (RdBu) are for data with a meaningful centre: change from baseline,
correlation. Set `vmin=-v, vmax=v` so that the centre is white.
jet (rainbow) creates bands that are not in the data, and its brightness goes up and down:
it is still in many medical software packages, and it should not be in your figures.
:::
78f126b2b7a2.fr:
## Cartes de couleurs

![](img/colormaps.png)

::: notes
Une carte de couleurs code un nombre ; l'œil doit le lire comme un nombre.
Les cartes séquentielles (viridis, la valeur par défaut ou grise) passent du foncé au clair : la luminosité augmente
avec la valeur, même imprimée en noir et blanc, et pour les lecteurs daltoniens (environ 1 homme
en 12).
Les cartes divergentes (RdBu) concernent les données avec un centre significatif : changement par rapport à la ligne de base,
corrélation. Réglez `vmin=-v, vmax=v` pour que le centre soit blanc.
jet (arc-en-ciel) crée des bandes qui ne sont pas dans les données, et sa luminosité augmente et diminue :
il figure encore dans de nombreux logiciels médicaux et ne devrait pas figurer dans vos figures.
:::

## The same values, four precisions

![](img/float_precision.png)

::: notes
Every number on this slide was computed by numpy, not typed by hand.
`float64` and `float32` agree to well beyond what a thermometer measures. `float16` starts
to show: 38.40625 instead of 38.4, harmless for a temperature, but the error grows with the
value (1000.4 becomes 1000.5: the gap between two float16 neighbours near 1000 is 0.5).
`float8` turns a 38.4 °C fever into 40 °C, and a platelet count of 1000 into "not a
number". It is a format for neural network weights, which tolerate noise, not for
clinical data.

80fc76b09815.en:
## Inheritance

![](img/inheritance.png)

::: notes
`class InPatient(Patient)` means "an InPatient is a Patient, plus a room". The class in
brackets is the parent (base class, superclass); the new one is the child, or subclass.
Everything defined on `Patient` is available on an `InPatient` without being written
again: the attributes set in `__init__`, `bmi()`, `add_heart_rate()`, `__repr__`.
`super().__init__(id, age, weight, height)` calls the parent's constructor, so the shared
attributes are set in one place, by the class that owns them. Forgetting that call is the
classic mistake: the object is created, and then `i.bmi()` fails with
`AttributeError: 'InPatient' object has no attribute 'weight'`, because nobody ever set
it.
`isinstance(i, Patient)` is True, and that is the whole point: code written for patients
works unchanged on inpatients. The reverse is False; an `InPatient` is a special case of
`Patient`, not the other way round. Prefer `isinstance(x, Patient)` to
`type(x) == Patient`, which answers False for every subclass and quietly breaks the idea.
A warning: inheritance is tempting and often wrong. Use it when the sentence "X is a Y" is
literally true; when X merely *has* a Y, store it as an attribute instead.
:::
80fc76b09815.fr:
## Héritage

![](img/inheritance.png)

::: notes
`class InPatient(Patient)` signifie « un patient hospitalisé est un patient plus une chambre ». La classe en

## Tuples: `tuple`

```python
blood_pressure = (120, 80)
systolic, diastolic = blood_pressure

blood_pressure[0] = 130   # TypeError

x, y = 1, 2
x, y = y, x               # swap
```

::: notes
A tuple is a fixed group of values that belong together: a blood pressure, a (row, col)
coordinate, a (min, max) range. Fixed is the point: nobody can change one half of a blood
pressure by accident.
Unpacking gives each part a name, and it is everywhere: `for key, value in d.items()`,
functions returning several values, the swap idiom.
Being immutable, a tuple can be a dict key; a list cannot.
:::

```python
class InPatient(Patient):
    def __init__(self, id, age, weight, height, room):
        super().__init__(id, age, weight, height)
        self.room = room

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"InPatient {self.id}, room {self.room}"

i = InPatient("P003", 71, 95.2, 1.70, room=12)
i.bmi()      # not on InPatient -> found on Patient
i            # InPatient('P003', room 12)
```

::: notes
The rule is one line: Python looks for the name on the object's own class first, then on
its parent, then on *its* parent, up to `object`; the first one found wins.
`i.bmi()` is not defined on `InPatient`, so Python walks up and runs the one on `Patient`.
`repr(i)` is defined on both, so the child's version wins: that is *overriding*.
An overridden method can still reuse the one it replaced: `super().__repr__()` inside the
child calls the parent's version, which is how you extend behaviour instead of copying it.
Same idea as `super().__init__`, which is nothing more than an overridden `__init__`
calling the original.
The payoff is *polymorphism*: one loop over a mixed list of `Patient` and `InPatient`
objects calls `p.bmi()` on each, and each object runs the right version. No test on the
type anywhere, which is exactly the `if` ladder that rots when a new case appears.
Debugging habit: when a method does not do what they expect, ask which class it came from.
`type(i).__mro__` prints the search order, `help(InPatient)` shows what was inherited and
what was redefined.
:::

## Boolean masks

![](img/masks.png)

::: notes
A comparison on an array gives an array of booleans of the same shape: the mask. Indexing
with a mask keeps the positions where it is True; the result is always 1D.
This is how you filter without a loop, and exactly how pandas filters rows later
(`df[df["bmi"] >= 30]`).
Combine conditions with `&` and `|`, not `and` / `or`, and parenthesise each condition:
`(bmi >= 18.5) & (bmi < 25)`. Forgetting the parentheses is the error of the week.
`np.where(cond, a, b)` picks from `a` where True and from `b` elsewhere, e.g. to clip
negative values to 0.
:::

## A lint check, safe and unsafe

```python
import os
# F401 unused import   -> safe fix
import pandas as pd

def mean_hr(path):
    df = pd.read_csv(path)
    n = len(df)
    # F841 unused variable -> unsafe fix
    return df["hr"].mean()

```

```bash

$ ruff check vitals.py
# Found 2 errors:
# * 1 fixable with `--fix`
# * 1 unsafe fix available with `--fix --unsafe-fixes`
```

::: notes
Two real findings on seven lines, and they are not equally safe to repair.
`F401 os imported but unused`: the import does nothing, so deleting the line cannot
change the result. Ruff marks that fix **safe**, and `ruff check --fix vitals.py`
removes it for you (and sorts the remaining imports, `I001`).
`F841 local variable n is assigned to but never used`: here ruff's fix is to drop the
`n =` and keep the call, `len(df)`. It marks it **unsafe**, because the right-hand side
might be doing something: `n = log_access(patient_id)` would still be called, but
`n = df.pop("hr")` changes `df`, and deleting the whole line would change the result.
Ruff refuses to guess. So `--fix` leaves it alone and tells you a `--unsafe-fixes` is
available; you only get it with `ruff check --fix --unsafe-fixes .`, and then you read
the diff before committing.
The rule for the room: `--fix` can run unattended, even in a hook. `--unsafe-fixes` is
something you run yourself, on a clean working tree, and check with `git diff`.
Also note F841 is often a real bug, not untidiness: the variable you computed and forgot
to return, or a typo where you assigned `mena` and used `mean`. Do not auto-delete the
evidence, read it.
:::

## Smaller is lighter and faster

![](img/dtype_memory.png)

::: notes
Memory is bytes per value times number of values. One CT volume is 79 million voxels:
629 MB in `float64`, 315 MB in `float32`. A batch of scans for training does not fit on a
GPU in `float64`.
Fewer bytes also means faster: more values per memory transfer, and GPUs have dedicated
hardware for 16 and 8 bit arithmetic. This is why deep learning trains in `float32` or
"mixed precision" (`float16`/`bfloat16` for the bulk, `float32` where it matters), and runs
large models in 8 bits or less.
The rule for this course: `float64` for statistics and tables, `float32` for images and
neural networks, smaller only when a library does it for you.
:::

## Format, and check

```bash
# format one file
$ ruff format clean.py
# format everything, recursively
$ ruff format .

# report, but change nothing
$ ruff format --check .
# lint: find likely mistakes
$ ruff check .
# lint, and fix what is safe
$ ruff check --fix .
```

::: notes
Three commands to remember, and the difference between them is the whole point.
`ruff format <path>` rewrites the file in place and prints `1 file reformatted`. A
directory (`.` is the current one) means every `.py` file below it; files listed in
`.gitignore` are skipped, so `.venv/` is not touched.
`--check` is the read-only version: it lists the files that *would* change and exits with
a non-zero status if there are any. That is exactly what you put in a pull-request check
or a git hook: it fails the build instead of silently editing the author's code.
`ruff check` is the linter, a different command from `format`; `--fix` applies only the
corrections ruff considers safe.
Practical advice: run `ruff format .` once at the start of a project, commit that as
"format with ruff" on its own, and from then on every diff stays small. Doing it in the
middle of a feature branch produces a 400-line commit that hides the one line that
matters.
Demonstrate live on `clean.py` from the notebook: `ruff format --check clean.py`, then
`ruff format clean.py`, then `git diff`.
:::

## Working with text

```python
raw = "  Diabetes Type 2 \n"
raw.strip()       # "Diabetes Type 2"
raw.strip().lower().replace(" ", "_")
                  # "diabetes_type_2"
"Ada Lovelace".split()
                  # ["Ada", "Lovelace"]
bmi = 22.857142
f"BMI: {bmi:.2f}" # "BMI: 22.86"
```

::: notes
This slide is data cleaning in miniature. Free text from a hospital system comes with
stray spaces, mixed case and line breaks; `strip`, `lower` and `replace` normalise it
so that "Diabetes Type 2" and "diabetes type 2 " count as the same diagnosis.
Methods chain because each returns a new string.
f-strings are the way to build text from values: `{bmi:.2f}` means "two decimals".
They replace `"BMI: " + str(bmi)`, which is longer and does not format.
:::

:::

## Loading a table

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("../data/patients.csv")
df.head()
df.shape      # (240, 7)
df.dtypes     # one type per column
df.info()     # types and the number of values present
```

::: notes
`pd.read_csv` is one line for what took a `csv.DictReader` loop, a list of dicts and a
manual conversion of every field. It also reads Excel (`read_excel`), JSON, SQL and others,
with the same shape of call.
Useful arguments when the export does not cooperate: `sep=";"` (the French Excel default),
`decimal=","`, `na_values=["", "NA", "NR"]`, `parse_dates=["admission"]`,
`encoding="latin-1"`.
`df.info()` is the one that tells you how many values are actually present per column, so
how many are missing.
:::

## Names can change type

```python
x = 42          # an int
x = "42"        # now a str
x + 1           # TypeError

```

::: notes
Dynamic typing: the label moved to a new value, of a new type. Python allowed the
reassignment, but it still refuses to mix types that make no sense together.
Read the error message out loud with them. Python errors name the types involved, and
learning to read that line is half of debugging.

```python
bmi = weight / height ** 2   # 200 at once
bmi.mean(), bmi.min(), bmi.max()

(bmi >= 30).mean()     # 0.215

cat = np.digitize(bmi, [18.5, 25, 30])
```

## The `ndarray`: shape and dtype

![](img/ndarray.png)

::: notes
Two attributes describe every array, and they are the first thing to print when something
goes wrong. `.shape` is a tuple, the size along each axis; `.ndim` is its length. `.dtype`
is the single type of every cell.
Axis 0 is the rows (going down), axis 1 the columns (going across). A table of 200
patients by 3 measurements has shape `(200, 3)`.
One float in the list and every cell becomes a float: the array picks a dtype that fits
every value. A string in the list would make an array of strings, and arithmetic stops
working, a classic symptom of a dirty CSV column.
:::
ba7649a02fa5.fr:
## Le `ndarray` : forme et type

![](img/ndarray.png)

::: notes
Deux attributs décrivent chaque tableau, et ils sont la première chose à imprimer lorsque quelque chose
ça va mal. `.shape` est un tuple, la taille le long de chaque axe ; `.ndim` est sa longueur. `.dtype`
est le type unique de chaque cellule.
L'axe 0 représente les lignes (descendant), l'axe 1 les colonnes (traversant). Une table de 200
les patients par 3 mesures ont la forme `(200, 3)`.
Un flottant dans la liste et chaque cellule devient un flottant : le tableau sélectionne un type qui correspond

fonctionne, un symptôme classique d’une colonne CSV sale.
:::

## `break` and `continue`

![](img/break_continue.png)

::: notes
`break` leaves the loop immediately: the search is over, the remaining items are never
looked at. This is how you find the first abnormal value without scanning the rest.
`continue` abandons the current turn only and goes on to the next: the idiom for skipping
missing values, which in real exports is most of the work.
Both work in `for` and in `while`. Keep them for cases that read as "stop" or "skip":
nested in three levels of `if`, they become unreadable.
:::
bbdc5ef3be88.fr:
## `break` et `continue`

![](img/break_continue.png)

::: notes
`break` quitte immédiatement la boucle : la recherche est terminée, les éléments restants ne sont jamais
regardé. C'est ainsi que vous trouvez la première valeur anormale sans analyser le reste.
`continue` abandonne uniquement le tour en cours et passe au suivant : l'idiome pour sauter
valeurs manquantes, ce qui représente l'essentiel du travail dans les exportations réelles.
Les deux fonctionnent en `for` et en `while`. Conservez-les pour les cas qui se lisent comme « stop » ou « saut » :
imbriqués dans trois niveaux de `if`, ils deviennent illisibles.

bf89711994d6.en:
## Inside a float

![](img/float_bits.png)

::: notes
A float is scientific notation in binary: a sign, an exponent (where the point goes: the
range) and a mantissa (the significant digits: the precision).
Halving the size costs both. `float32` keeps 7 digits, plenty for any measurement made in a
hospital. `float16` keeps 3 digits and cannot go above 65 504. `float8` keeps about one
digit; it exists for deep learning on recent GPUs (two variants: e4m3 for precision,
e5m2 for range).
NumPy itself stops at `float16`: `float8` comes from the `ml_dtypes` package or from
`torch.float8_e4m3fn`.
:::
bf89711994d6.fr:
## À l'intérieur d'un float

![](img/float_bits.png)

::: notes
Un flottant est une notation scientifique en binaire : un signe, un exposant (là où va le point : le
plage) et une mantisse (les chiffres significatifs : la précision).
Réduire de moitié la taille coûte aux deux. `float32` conserve 7 chiffres, ce qui est suffisant pour toute mesure effectuée dans un
hôpital. `float16` conserve 3 chiffres et ne peut pas dépasser 65 504. `float8` conserve environ un
chiffre; il existe pour le deep learning sur les GPU récents (deux variantes : e4m3 pour la précision,
e5m2 pour la gamme).
NumPy lui-même s'arrête à `float16` : `float8` vient du package `ml_dtypes` ou de
`torch.float8_e4m3fn`.
:::

## First figure

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(t, temp, label="temperature")
ax.axhline(38, ls="--", label="fever")
ax.set_xlabel("time (h)")
ax.set_ylabel("temperature (°C)")
ax.set_title("Patient P0001")
ax.legend()
fig.savefig("temp.png", dpi=200)
```

::: notes
The pattern of every figure in this course: create the figure and its axes, draw on the
axes, label the axes, save the figure.
`plt.subplots()` returns two things, unpacked into `fig` and `ax` (tuple unpacking, from
Session 1).
You will also see the short style `plt.plot(...)`, `plt.xlabel(...)`: it draws on "the
current axes". It is fine for a quick look, but as soon as there are two plots it becomes
ambiguous. Use `fig, ax` everywhere and you never have to wonder.
In a notebook the figure is displayed at the end of the cell; in a script, call
`plt.show()` or just save it.
:::

## NumPy data types

| dtype | bytes | holds | typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bool` | 1 | `True` / `False` | masks |
| `uint8` | 1 | 0 to 255 | image pixels |
| `int16` | 2 | -32 768 to 32 767 | CT scans (Hounsfield units) |
| `int64` | 8 | about ±9.2e18 | counts, ids (the default int) |
| `float16` | 2 | ~3 digits, up to 65 504 | deep learning |
| `float32` | 4 | ~7 digits | images, deep learning, GPUs |
| `float64` | 8 | ~16 digits | statistics (the default float) |

::: notes
Python has one `int` and one `float`. NumPy has a family of each, with a fixed size in
bytes, because every cell of an array must have the same size for the block of memory to
work.
The number in the name is the number of bits: `int16` is 16 bits, 2 bytes. `u` means
unsigned (no negative values).
You rarely pick: `np.array` chooses `int64` or `float64`. But the files you read pick for
you: a DICOM CT is usually `int16`, a PNG `uint8`, a NIfTI often `float32`, and a deep
learning model `float32` or less. Always print `.dtype` after loading data.
:::

## Local and remote

![](img/git_remote.png)

::: notes
git works entirely on your machine: commit on a train, without network. A remote is
another copy of the repository, usually on GitHub (or GitLab, or the hospital's own
server). `git clone` makes your copy once; `git push` sends your new commits;
`git pull` fetches the others' commits and merges them into yours.
GitHub adds what git does not have: a web page for the project, issues to track bugs,
pull requests to review a change before it is merged. The course material lives there.
Two people editing the same lines produce a conflict: git marks both versions in the
file, you choose, then commit. It is a normal event, not an error.
:::

d9c79b2f5bb5.en:
## Creating a snapshot

![](img/git_areas.png)

::: notes
The one mental model to get right. You edit files in the working folder as usual.
`git add` chooses which changes go into the next snapshot (the staging area). `git commit`
records that snapshot in the repository, the hidden `.git/` folder.
Why the middle step: you changed three files but only two belong to the same fix. Stage
those two, commit, then stage and commit the third with its own message.
`git status` is the command to type when lost: it says what is in each area, and
usually suggests the next command.
:::
d9c79b2f5bb5.fr:
## Création d'un instantané

![](img/git_areas.png)

::: notes
Le seul modèle mental pour réussir. Vous modifiez les fichiers dans le dossier de travail comme d'habitude.
`git add` choisit les modifications qui seront apportées à l'instantané suivant (la zone de préparation). `git commit`
enregistre cet instantané dans le référentiel, le dossier caché `.git/`.
Pourquoi l'étape intermédiaire : vous avez modifié trois fichiers mais seulement deux appartiennent au même correctif. Scène
ces deux-là, validez, puis mettez en scène et validez le troisième avec son propre message.
`git status` est la commande à taper en cas de perte : elle indique ce qu'il y a dans chaque zone, et
suggère généralement la commande suivante.
:::

## Choosing and converting

```python
x = np.arange(4, dtype=np.float32)
x.dtype, x.nbytes        # float32, 16
x.astype(np.float16)     # convert: a copy

np.array([250], dtype=np.uint8) + 10
                         # [4], not 260
np.float16(70000)        # inf: overflow

h = np.full(10000, 0.1, dtype=np.float16)
h.cumsum()[-1]           # 256.0, not 1000
```

::: notes
`dtype=` at creation, `.astype()` to convert (it returns a new array), `.nbytes` for the
memory.
Three silent failures, none of which raises an error:
(1) integers wrap around: 250 + 10 in `uint8` is 4. Typical when adjusting the brightness
  of an image; convert to a larger type first.
(2) `float16` overflows to `inf` above 65 504.
(3) adding many small numbers in low precision stalls: at 256 the next 0.1 is below half
  the gap between float16 neighbours (0.25), so the sum stops growing. Accumulate in
  `float32` or `float64` (numpy's `.sum()` already protects you better than a running
  total, but not completely).
:::

## Strings: `str`

![](img/string_index.png)

::: notes
A string is a sequence of characters, and sequences share one indexing grammar that they
will reuse for lists, tuples, numpy arrays and pandas: indices start at 0, negative indices
count from the end, and a slice `[start:stop]` excludes `stop`.
`name[:3]` is "the first three", `name[-1]` "the last one": say these as sentences.
Strings are immutable: you never change a string, you build a new one. That is why every
string method returns a result instead of modifying the string in place.
:::

sera réutilisé pour les listes, les tuples, les tableaux numpy et les pandas : les indices commencent à 0, les indices négatifs
comptez à partir de la fin, et une tranche `[start:stop]` exclut `stop`.

## Understanding with a plot

![](img/anscombe.png)

::: notes
Anscombe's quartet (1973). Four datasets of 11 points: same mean, same variance, same
correlation, same regression line, to two decimals. A table of summary statistics says they
are identical.
The plots say: a noisy linear relation, a curve, a perfect line with one outlier, and no
relation at all except one extreme point.
The habit to build: plot the raw data before any statistic. In clinical data the plot is
where you find the impossible ages, the unit changes (kg vs lb), the duplicated rows and
the device that was unplugged.
:::

::: notes
Le quatuor d'Anscombe (1973). Quatre ensembles de données de 11 points : même moyenne, même variance, même
corrélation, même droite de régression, à deux décimales. Un tableau de statistiques récapitulatives indique qu'ils
sont identiques.
Les tracés indiquent : une relation linéaire bruyante, une courbe, une ligne parfaite avec une valeur aberrante, et non
relation du tout sauf un point extrême.
L'habitude à prendre : tracer les données brutes avant toute statistique. Dans les données cliniques, le tracé est
